'''''Populus'' × ''canadensis''''', known as the '''hybrid black poplar''', '''Canadian poplar''' or '''Carolina poplar''', is an artificial [[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] between ''[[Populus nigra]]'' from Europe and ''[[Populus deltoides]]'' from North America, which arose when the two parent species were first brought together in cultivation in France soon after 1700.<ref name="Mitchell1">{{cite book | last1=Mitchell | first1=Alan F. | last2=Mitchell | first2=Alan | title=Alan Mitchell's Trees of Britain | publisher=Whitman Publishing & Distribution Company | date=1996 | isbn=0-00-219972-6 | pages=273–278}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Populus+x+canadensis|title=Populus x canadensis Canadian Poplar, Carolina Poplar PFAF Plant Database|website=www.pfaf.org|access-date=2016-04-18}}</ref> It is a vigorous, broadly columnar, [[deciduous]] tree growing to {{convert|40|–|45|m|ft|abbr=on}}, which is commonly used in [[Tree plantation|plantation forestry]] and by landscape architects. The tallest reliably measured, near the [[Weltenburg Abbey]] in [[Kelheim]], Germany, is 47 metres tall, and the stoutest, in [[Baak]] in the Netherlands, is 8.5 metres girth.<ref name="MT">{{cite web | title=The thickest, tallest, and oldest Hybrid Black Poplars (Populus × canadensis) | website=Monumental trees | url=https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/trees/canadianpoplar/records/ | access-date=2025-08-05}}</ref>

==Description==
It is intermediate between its parents in characters, with leaves deltoid (triangular) but with a less broad base than ''P. deltoides'' and often somewhat acute at the base, as in ''P. nigra''; the leaves are 8–14 cm long and 8–11 cm wide. As with all poplars, it is [[dioecy|dioecious]], with separate male and female trees; the sex of an individual is often an important clue to identifying which [[cultivar]] it is. The pollen catkins are red, the seed catkins green, and opening when mature to shed their small seeds embedded in cotton-like fluff.<ref name="Mitchell2">{{cite book | last=Mitchell | first=Alan F. | title=A Field Guide to the Trees of Britain and Northern Europe | publisher=Collins | publication-place=London | date=1974 | isbn=0-00-212035-6 | pages=186–187}}</ref>

===Cultivars===
Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been selected, mostly for forestry use; the most significant listed below in order of naming:<ref name="Mitchell1"/><ref name="Mitchell2"/>
*'Serotina' 1750, France. From Latin, "late", named from its late leaf bud opening, not until late May or June; the first produced, it is very vigorous, and easily recognised by its slanting trunk and few, large branches. Male. To 42 m tall.<ref name="Mitchell1"/>
*'Marilandica' 1800. An early clone, now rarely found. Female. To 40 m tall.<ref name="Mitchell1"/>
*'Regenerata' ('''railway poplar''') 1814, France. From Latin, "regenerating", as it [[pollarding|pollards]] well; the English name from being much planted along railway lines in England in the 20th century. Leafs out a month earlier than 'Serotina', but similar in crown shape. Female. To 40 m tall.<ref name="Mitchell1"/><ref name="Mitchell2"/>
*'Eugenei' 1832, Metz, France. One parent was ''Populus nigra'' 'Italica' (Lombardy poplar), and it inherits a narrow crown from this, though much less obvious than its parent. Male.<ref name="Mitchell2"/>
*'Serotina Aurea' (syn. 'Aurea'; '''golden poplar'''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://trusttrees.org.au/tree/VIC/Melbourne/Royal_Botanic_Gardens_Birdwood_Avenue_30|title=Golden Poplar|website=National Trust (Australia)|accessdate=31 May 2019}}</ref>) 1871, Belgium. From Latin, "gold", referring to the yellowish foliage. Slower-growing, and only reaching around 30 m.<ref name="Mitchell2"/> It has won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/68970/Populus-x-canadensis-Aurea/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Populus'' × ''canadensis'' 'Aurea' | accessdate = 14 May 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 82 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 14 May 2018}}</ref>
*'Robusta' 1895, France. From Latin, "robust, fast-growing". A much straighter tree than 'Serotina', growing vertical, and with more numerous but smaller and more regular branching and narrow-crowned; very vigorous when young (2–2.5 m per year). Important in forestry. Male.<ref name="Mitchell1"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://davisla.wordpress.com/2013/06/19/plant-of-the-week-populus-x-canadensis-robusta/|title=Populus x canadensis 'Robusta'|website=landscape architect's pages|date=19 June 2013 |access-date=2016-04-18}}</ref>
*'Gelrica' c.1900, Netherlands. Male. Particularly vigorous in trunk diameter growth; the stoutest known specimen is this cultivar.<ref name="MT"/>

==Ecology==
Hybrid black poplar is very susceptible to attack by [[Viscum album|mistletoe]] (''Viscum album''), to which its European parent ''P. nigra'' is highly resistant; heavy mistletoe infestation on a poplar is a reliable indicator that the poplar is ''P. × canadensis'' and not ''P. nigra''.<ref>{{cite web | title=Leitfaden für das genetische Monitoring Schwarz-Pappel (''Populus nigra'' L.) | url=https://www.lwf.bayern.de/mam/cms02/asp/dateien/lifegenmon_leitfaden_pappeln.pdf |language=de | access-date=2025-08-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Kołodziejek | first1=Jeremi | last2=Patykowski | first2=Jacek | last3=Kołodziejek | first3=Rafał | title=Distribution, frequency and host patterns of European mistletoe (Viscum album subsp. album) in the major city of Lodz, Poland | journal=Biologia | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=68 | issue=1 | date=2012-12-27 | issn=0006-3088 | doi=10.2478/s11756-012-0128-4 | doi-access=free | pages=55–64 | url=http://www.degruyter.com/downloadpdf/j/biolog.2013.68.issue-1/s11756-012-0128-4/s11756-012-0128-4.xml | access-date=2025-08-05| url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=M. |last2=Crampin |first2=J. |title=The native Black Poplar in Somerset, particularly in Taunton Deane |journal=Somerset Archaeology and Natural History |date=1994 |volume=138 |pages=235–245 |url=https://sanhs.org/wp-content/uploads/19-AndersonCrampin.pdf |access-date=5 August 2025}}</ref>
